work_packages.name: A game selects a 2D scene, and sprites reach the screen through the game's own frame with no sky, shadow or light work, on the Mac and in Chrome

items.statement: On the Mac, on both native recipes, frame rows of an embedded test sheet drawn at whole-number scales of 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 on the pixel grid leave the frame as their source texels: every submitted pixel of an opaque texel is that texel's 8-bit colour, each texel a clean block, at even and odd output extents and where a sprite crosses an edge of the view. World Y is up and nothing is mirrored.
items.ask: Read the test. Is the reference image built on the CPU from the sheet's source texels and the design's view rule, without any of the renderer's shaders? Does it compare every pixel of the submitted SDR output at each of the five scales, on the portable and the Apple tile recipe, at an odd extent, with a sprite cut by each edge of the view and an asymmetric sprite that would show a flip?

items.statement: A 2D scene prepared with no contribution compiles to its sprite pass and the output half's passes and nothing else. Its generation allocates no sky table, cascade, cluster, depth, motion, reactive, mesh, star or reconstruction resource and creates none of their pipelines, its resolved selections name no reconstructor, and a completed frame's timing names no 3D pass. The same test finds each of those in a 3D scene.
items.ask: Is the expected pass list written out in the test and compared whole? Does the storage check walk everything the generation allocated, and does the 3D control, on a recipe that resolves a reconstructor, prove the check would see such a resource or selection if a 2D scene had one?

items.statement: A request only a 3D scene can meet is refused when a 2D scene is prepared, with an error that names it: a contribution that declares a shadow, opaque or after-opaque stage; temporal sampling; a culling mode; and a reconstructor asked for by name, wherever the frame runtime lets a game or a run ask for one. A contribution with only upload and simulate stages attaches and runs, and adds only its own passes at those stages to the pass list of WP1.2. The game can read which scene kind was prepared.
items.ask: Is there one refusal test for each request, each asserting a named error and an unchanged scene? Is any of them accepted and ignored instead? If the frame runtime offers no way to ask for a reconstructor by name, is that shown, with where the builder looked?

items.statement: Every existing 3D scene variant compiles to the same pass order, attachment storage and transient slots as before this work package, on both recipes.
items.ask: Is the 'before' side taken from main at the commit this work package started from, for the variants the V1 game prepares, and not produced by the changed code?

items.statement: Through the display-referred transfer, an opaque texel of each of the 256 grey codes and of a set of saturated colours leaves the frame as the same 8-bit code, with no dither. A half-transparent texel over a known background equals the linear-light blend to within one code. A value above 1 is kept in the scene-linear checkpoint and clips at white, channel by channel, in SDR output.
items.ask: Does the test run on both native recipes and read the submitted SDR bytes and the scene-linear checkpoint through engine capture's tap? Is the one-code allowance used only for blended texels, with opaque texels compared exactly? Are the 3D scene's two tone operators and its dither unchanged?

items.statement: After a resize to another extent, a change of density, a discarded frame, a refused surface, a capture frame and a replaced device, a 2D scene draws exactly what a fresh scene draws at that extent, with the sprite target at the surface's pixel extent and no resource of an old generation in use.
items.ask: Is each of the six events driven through the host's own calls, and is the fresh scene's image compared pixel for pixel after each?

items.statement: In Chrome the V1 game's sprite scene draws its test card exactly as the CPU reference at whole-number scales, compiles no 3D pass, follows a canvas resize, and draws again on a replaced device.
On the Mac the sprite scene's test card reads as drawn: upright, unmirrored, colours as authored, flat blocks of colour with hard edges, nothing missing and nothing 3D behind it.
items.inspect: Capture `fixed` stills of the sprite scene with T2 engine capture at 1280×720 and at 3456×2234, at scales of 2 and 4. Judge each frame whole and in native-size crops of the card's lines, colour ramps and marks.

items.statement: On the Mac, CPU and GPU times for the sprite scene are on record at 1920×1080 and at 3456×2234, with the sprite pass, tone and present apart and the bytes of each target, from two separate runs with build and load. The valley route is timed before and after this work package with no 2D scene. Each tripwire the design names is flagged. The figures are baselines: no time decides the result.
items.ask: Were both retained runs release builds of the claimed commit, with the load on the machine recorded? Does the command succeed or fail on the record being complete, and never on a time? Is the valley's paired figure from the same route and build settings on both sides?

items.statement: In Chrome, CPU and GPU times for the sprite scene are on record at 1920×1080 and at the page's full backing size, from two separate runs with build and load, with the limits Chrome's capability record reports for sampled textures, array layers and storage buffers. Each tripwire is flagged. The figures are baselines: no time decides the result.
Every registered exact baseline, on the Mac and in Chrome, passes the verifier at the claimed commit: this work package moved no retained image.

work_packages.quality_bar: A 2D path as separate from 3D as Bevy's `core_2d`, Godot's canvas renderer or Unity's 2D Renderer: a 2D game prepares and runs nothing 3D, and a request it cannot meet is refused by name. As exact as a pixel-art game shown at a whole-number scale, such as Celeste: every texel is a clean block of its authored colour.

work_packages.name: Ten thousand sprites follow the simulation, gliding between ticks in an overlap order that holds still

items.statement: A world row is drawn at the pose between its two tick endpoints that the frame's alpha names, in position, rotation by the shorter arc and scale: at alphas of 0, 0.25, 0.5 and 1 its pixels are where a CPU reference puts them. A repeated tick and a pause change nothing. A row whose identity or slot generation was not extracted at the previous tick, or whose timeline changed, is drawn at its committed pose with no slide.
items.ask: Read the test. Does it cover a slot reused by a new entity within one tick, a rewind onto a new timeline, and a rotation that crosses the wrap from one side of a turn to the other?

items.statement: With no band, rows are drawn back to front by layer, then sort value, then stable identity, world rows and frame rows together: for overlapping rows of known colours, the colour read at every overlap is the one that order puts on top, across uploads that change other rows, with equal sort values and reused slots. A frame row at an equal layer and sort value is in front of every world row.
items.ask: Does the test read pixels back at the overlaps, and not the order list? Are there rows with equal sort values whose order only identity decides, and does it run for many ticks while other rows change?

items.statement: Tint, flash, transparency and additive sprites, interleaved in one pass in any order, give the pixels that a CPU blend of the same rows in the same order gives, to within one code: a normal sprite over an additive one over a normal one is three layers in that order.
items.ask: Is the CPU blend written from the design's rules for tint, flash and additive, without the renderer's shader? Does a case put an additive sprite between two normal ones?

items.statement: The sprite pass records one draw for the whole frame however many sheets, layers and blends its rows mix, with eight sheets bound; a ninth sheet is refused at preparation by name. A tick uploads the rows that changed and the order list, and nothing for a row that did not change. A row beyond the declared capacity, or with a value that is not finite, is dropped and counted.
items.ask: Is the draw count taken from the recorded pass, with rows from all eight sheets interleaved in order? Are uploaded bytes counted where they are written, and compared with the rows that changed?

items.statement: A row whose frame the game advances by tick shows each frame for exactly the ticks it was set, on a display running at twice the tick rate: no frame is skipped, shown early or repeated out of order, and a pause holds the frame.

On the Mac the sprite scene draws the V1 game's 10,000 simulated entities as world rows through the game's ordinary host: 10,000 rows accepted and none dropped, its movers interpolated, one sprite draw, no 3D pass, and frame rows drawn among them.
items.ask: Do the rows come from the tick page through the game's scene source, on the game's own world lane, and not from a list built for the test?

items.statement: In Chrome the sprite scene draws the same 10,000 entities as world rows with one sprite draw and no 3D pass, none dropped, its movers interpolated.

In real time on the Mac the movers glide: no sprite steps at the tick rate, jumps, or slides in from elsewhere. Where sprites overlap the same one stays in front. A flashed sprite turns the flash colour inside its own outline, and an additive one glows without hiding what is behind it.
items.inspect: Capture the sprite scene's field at 1920×1080 with T2 engine capture in `realtime` mode for at least twenty seconds, with movers crossing each other and with flashed, tinted and additive sprites among them. Judge consecutive frames at 1x, whole and in native-size crops of single movers and of overlaps.

items.statement: In real time in Chrome the movers glide and overlaps hold still, as on the Mac.
items.inspect: Capture the same field in Chrome with T2 engine capture in `realtime` mode for at least twenty seconds. Judge consecutive frames at 1x, whole and in native-size crops of single movers and of overlaps.

items.statement: On the Mac, with 2,000, 5,000 and 10,000 world rows whose pose changes every tick, extraction, ordering, upload bytes, the sprite pass's GPU time and the whole frame are on record at 1920×1080 and at 3456×2234, with shaded pixels beside each time, from two separate runs with build and load. Each tripwire is flagged. The figures are baselines: no time decides the result.
items.ask: Were both retained runs release builds of the claimed commit, with the load on the machine recorded? Does the command succeed or fail on the record being complete, and never on a time? Does every row's pose really change every tick in these runs, so that every row is uploaded?

items.statement: In Chrome, with 2,000, 5,000 and 10,000 world rows whose pose changes every tick, extraction, ordering, upload bytes, the sprite pass's GPU time and the whole frame are on record, with shaded pixels beside each time, from two separate runs with build and load. Each tripwire is flagged. The figures are baselines: no time decides the result.
Every registered exact baseline, on the Mac and in Chrome, passes the verifier at the claimed commit: this work package moved no retained image.

With a band set, the order is one list kept from tick to tick. Two world rows that are near each other change their relative order only at a tick where the one moving in front has a sort value more than the band above the other's. After every tick, no two rows next to each other in the list are waiting to exchange: near ones are within the band of true order and the rest in exact order. A row with no valid history is placed in exact order with the rows on either side of it, and frame rows by the exact key.
items.ask: Read the test. Does it replay the design's travelling pair and its chain of three, and read the pair's overlap back as pixels? Does a long randomized run, with three or more rows overlapping at once, spawns, despawns and reused slots, check every change of relative order between rows with history against the rule, with code that does not share the order's own update? Does the same run fail an order made by sorting a held value for each row?

work_packages.quality_bar: Crowd motion and layering as in Vampire Survivors and Halls of Torment: thousands of bodies glide between simulation ticks at the display's refresh, and where two overlap the same one stays in front from frame to frame. Effects as in those games: a hit flashes the whole sprite, a glow adds light without hiding what is behind it.

work_packages.name: Sprites stay crisp at every window size and pixel density, and nothing shimmers when the view scrolls

items.statement: The creation-counters scene_2d generation inventory passes on both Metal recipes for its one-frame sheet, whose padded atlas is 12 by 12 and whose SpriteFrameRecord occupies 32 bytes. The test still witnesses the live 2D storage, allocations, pipelines and submitted passes against its 3D control. Guard: existing main-tier generation inventory.
items.check: THRUM_REQUIRE_GPU=1 cargo test --locked --offline -p thrum-render --features creation-counters --test scene_2d generation_prepares_only_the_sprite_and_output_resources -- --exact

items.statement: On both Metal recipes and Chrome WebGPU, the existing sprite draw at the output extent applies the widened pixel filter near 1.5× and a frame-local spatial reconstruction through the off-grid 2× edge crossings. At aligned 2× it selects the authored texels. Record the before-and-after sprite-pass timings for the 1920×1080 1.5× scroll on Metal and Chrome, with recipe, device, shaded pixels, overdraw and load.
items.ask: At 1.5× does the shader combine premultiplied scene-linear RGBA with normalized, nonnegative weights within mechanism 6's support? At 2× does it use continuous projected texel coordinates through single-axis and two-axis texel-edge crossings and converge to the authored sample at alignment? Do the standalone quad margin and transparent gutter cover the chosen footprint, and do tiles use their own extruded edges with unchanged shared-edge ownership?

items.statement: On both Metal recipes, one axis-aligned bright marker per scale at 1.25×, 1.5× and 2.37× follows a diagonal camera sweep over 256 subpixel poses while its row stays fixed. The submitted scene-linear marker centroid moves in the requested direction on both axes between the start, quarter, half, three-quarter and end checkpoints. A frozen-view control fails that movement test. Record: submitted camera sweep.
items.check: THRUM_REQUIRE_GPU=1 cargo test --locked --offline -p thrum-render --test sprite_crisp fractional_camera_scroll -- --nocapture
items.ask: Does each sweep hold the row fixed and advance the ordinary sprite view through distinct submissions? Does the proof read the marker positions from those images and reject the same pixels replayed at different expected poses?

items.statement: At aligned whole-number scales from 1× through 6×, the image is the authored texels repeated as pixel blocks. Scrolling an aligned view by whole output pixels translates the image by exactly that amount and preserves the translated texel bytes.

On both Metal recipes and both sheet kinds, the rotated white outline over white stays white, the isolated cyan witness contains no neighbouring colour, and two adjacent tiles show no background at their shared edge across the submitted edge suite's ten scales from 0.25× through 6× and sixteen offset poses. Record: submitted edge and atlas witnesses.
items.ask: From the actual uploaded frame placements, do contrasting frames face all four sides of the bleed witness on the same atlas page with only the intended gutter and padding between them, at each of the three uploaded mip levels? Does the submitted pixel test check the whole witness at the tested scales and reject the third colour at the shared tile edge?

items.statement: A smooth sheet's one-texel checker drawn at a scale of 0.25 is the flat mean of its two colours in linear light, to within one code, at every scroll offset.

The Mac sprite scene uses the built-in display's backing pixels one to one in real 640×360, 1280×720 and 1707×933 point windows. In each window and on the first presented submission after resize, the sprite target, viewport and drawable match the backing extent and the engine's submitted aligned card matches its authored texels. Record: AppKit geometry and windowed engine submissions.
items.ask: Does the unattended check verify shell geometry at the three sizes and after resize, record console state, and distinguish a presented sample from geometry alone using observed surface occlusion and no drawable? Does a complete real-window record covering the landed path link each presented submission, including the first after resize, to the matching engine pixels and exact card comparison by submission ID? A geometry-only result leaves the presentation proof open.

items.statement: In Chrome WebGPU at DPR 1 and 2, the canvas has one backing pixel for each device pixel and the aligned card is exact, both initially and after resizing. At both densities, the WP3.2 camera sweep over fixed rows passes the same submitted-marker movement test and frozen-view control at 1.25×, 1.5× and 2.37×. Record: canvas and submitted camera sweep.
items.ask: Is the camera centre advanced through successive submissions of the same retained scene at each scale, and does the pixel-based check reject a frozen camera even when the requested centres advance?

items.statement: On Metal through a slow diagonal pan and a fast scroll at 1.5×, 2× and 2.37×, the test card's original one-texel stripes and checker remain distinct with no visible contrast pulse or crawl at normal size and speed. Ground seams stay closed and rotating outlines stay clean.
items.inspect: Capture the existing 1920×1080 card, ground and rotating field with T2 engine capture in realtime mode, at 0.05 and 3 output pixels per simulation tick in X with the 0.53 diagonal Y component at each scale. Watch the original-speed whole frames and native-size crops through several subpixel cycles. Check that (1) both stripe orientations and the checker stay distinct and show no repeated fading, apparent thickening or sparkle, (2) no ground seam opens, and (3) rotating outlines stay clean. Use the first review's 1.5× take to locate the offending patches.

items.statement: On Metal, pixel sprites retain distinct fine marks and clean outlines at their still scales. Smooth sprites look clean over light and dark backgrounds, including at 0.25×.
items.inspect: Capture fixed stills with T2 engine capture at 640×360, 1920×1080 and 3456×2234. Inspect the existing pixel sprites at 1×, 1.5×, 2.37×, 4× and 6×, the original stripe and checker patches at 1.5×, and smooth sprites at 0.25×, 0.5×, 1× and 2× over light and dark backgrounds. Judge full frames and native-size crops. Check that (1) pixel art keeps distinct one-texel marks, square structure and clean outlines, and (2) smooth art has no fringe, halo, bleed or visible aliasing at quarter size.

items.statement: In Chrome WebGPU at DPR 1 and 2, the original one-texel stripes and checker remain distinct with no visible contrast pulse or crawl at normal size and speed in slow and fast scrolls at 1.5× and 2.37×. Ground seams stay closed and rotating outlines stay clean.
items.inspect: Capture the WP3.8 sprite route in T2 realtime mode at 1.5× and 2.37×, both speeds and both DPRs, holding the backing extent at 1920×1080. Watch the original-speed whole frames and native-size crops through several subpixel cycles. Check that (1) both stripe orientations and the checker stay distinct and show no repeated fading, apparent thickening or sparkle, (2) no ground seam opens, and (3) rotating outlines stay clean. Use the first review's Chrome takes to locate the offending patches.

work_packages.quality_bar: Pixel stability as in Celeste. At normal viewing size and recorded speed, fine lines and checks stay distinct and their contrast holds during the pan. Edges as clean as in Hades and Hollow Knight, with no fringe, halo, neighbouring sheet colour or gap between ground tiles. Judge the running output by eye.

work_packages.name: An artist saves a sprite sheet and the running game shows the new art in one frame, on the Mac and in Chrome

items.statement: A sheet folder cooks to one product for each profile: pages of one size as an array texture, and a frame table that returns every frame's name, page, rectangle, trim, source size, pivot and tile mark as authored, for single images and for grids. Texels are premultiplied in linear light. A pixel sheet is uncompressed on every profile. Cooking the same folder twice gives the same bytes. A frame larger than a page, a duplicate name and a description that names a missing file are each refused by name, and the previous product stays in the manifest.
items.ask: Read the test. Does it decode the cooked pages and compare each frame's texels with its source image, premultiplied, including a trimmed frame and a grid cell? Does it measure that the gutter between frames is wide enough for every mip level written?

items.statement: The runtime refuses a malformed sheet product before any of it is used, each with a named error: a truncated table, a rectangle outside its page, a page count that disagrees with the texture, a duplicate name, and a pivot or density that is not finite.

The 2D sprite pass draws cooked texels from a lease. Pending rows are absent and counted until the frame that records the last copy is submitted, after which the rows appear together. A 2D placement is refused by name. Once resident, two cooked animation frames with different trim origins keep their authored landmark anchored at the same row position. A cooked frame with the default centre and an embedded frame with the existing top-left anchor also land at their expected pixels. Guard: small Metal residency and sprite placement test.
items.ask: Does the test hold the last copy unsubmitted and show the pending sheet absent? In the submitted image, does it compare both cooked world-row frames against positions derived independently from untrimmed artwork, at the same row position with and without a quarter turn and signed scale flip? Do frame-row controls show the cooked default centre and the embedded top-left anchor? Does the sprite pass take pages only from the lease?

items.statement: Saving a changed image switches that sheet's pages and its frame table in one submitted frame: every frame of the edit window equals the all-old or the all-new reference, never a mix. A discarded switch frame commits nothing. Only the changed sheet's pages are uploaded, other sheets keep their textures by identity, and no pipeline or graph is created.
items.ask: Does the edit change both the pixels and the packing, so that new pixels under old rectangles would match neither reference?

items.statement: A frame handle taken by name keeps showing that name's picture after an edit adds, removes or repacks other frames. A name the current sheet lacks draws nothing and is counted in the frame's record, and draws again when a later save restores it.

A save that cannot be cooked or taken leaves the last good sheet on screen and names the reason: an image that does not parse, a frame larger than a page, a missing file, a sheet the device cannot hold, and a failed upload.
items.ask: Is each of the five failures injected by its own test, through the cooker or residency's own failure path?

items.statement: After the device is replaced, embedded sheets draw at once, cooked sheets are absent until they are staged again and then appear whole, and no view of the old device is used.

In Chrome the moving sprite scene draws a cooked sheet from the fetched store. After a save it fetches only the changed product and shows it in one switch while frames keep advancing. Record: fetched product, switch and elapsed-time motion.
items.inspect: Use the same Chrome edit that the check qualifies. Take T2 engine capture in realtime mode from moving frames before the save through the first submitted frame using the new sheet and the following motion. Review at 1x with the save time, monotonic submission times, committed ticks, view motion and skipped-opportunity records aligned to the switch. Does the scene keep moving through fetch and staging without a visible pause relative to the pre-save interval? A gap in submissions must remain visible in elapsed-time playback.

items.statement: On the Mac the moving sprite scene keeps advancing through a recolour and a save that repacks the sheet. At each switch every sprite takes the new art in one frame, with no blank, wrong or mixed picture. Record: elapsed-time motion and the two switches.
items.inspect: Capture the sprite field with a moving view using T2 engine capture in realtime mode. For each edit watch at 1x from ordinary pre-save motion through the first submitted frame using the new sheet and the following motion. Use the save time, monotonic submission times, committed ticks, view motion and skipped-opportunity records to check for a visible pause through cooking and staging against the pre-save interval. Preserve any submission gap in playback. Inspect the eight frames around each switch whole and in native-size crops for blanks, wrong art and a mix of old and new.

items.statement: The public sheet guide explains the folder, pixel and smooth sheet kinds, frame names, grid cells, tiles and linear-light blending. It shows how a cooked pivot is authored in original-frame texels, where its default centre is, and how the row position anchors it through trim. It states the embedded top-left convention.
items.ask: Does a folder and description written from the documentation alone cook and draw as it says, at the claimed commit?

work_packages.quality_bar: Sprite import as in Godot's or Unity's atlas workflow from Aseprite, without a restart or a hitch: save the art and the running game shows it a moment later, never half-swapped and never with the wrong picture on a sprite. A bad save leaves the last good art on screen and says why.

work_packages.name: The reference crowd of 10,000 is drawn on the Mac and in Chrome, the sprite scene works on the iPhone simulator, and a game maker can start a 2D scene from the guide

items.statement: On the Mac the crowd view draws SIM-2D's Crowd trace at 2,000, 5,000 and 10,000 bodies: every live body is a world row each tick, slots are reused and no row interpolates across a reuse, the frame is one sprite draw with no 3D pass, and the run ends at the digests SIM-2D retained, so drawing changed nothing in the world.
items.ask: Does the view depend on SIM-2D's rule package and draw through the public sprite interface only? Does the run report slots reused and rows that skipped interpolation, each above zero? Is the retained digest file SIM-2D's own, unchanged?

items.statement: In Chrome the crowd view draws the Crowd trace at the three sizes with every live body a world row, one sprite draw and no 3D pass, and ends at the retained digests.

The crowd's tick-to-tick jitter in sort value is measured and on record, and the band is set from it. With the band off and on, the record gives, for pairs that overlap on screen: reversals a tick, pairs that reverse and reverse back within 30 ticks, the share of pairs more than one band and more than two bands out of true order, and the worst pair. With the band on, every change of relative order between two near rows in the run obeyed the design's pair rule.
items.ask: Is the band the crowd view uses the value the record derives, with the reasoning stated? Are the counts taken over pairs that overlap on screen? Is the pair rule checked across the whole run by code that does not share the order's own update? Are the out-of-order figures recorded as measured, with none treated as a pass mark?

items.statement: On the Mac at 1920×1080 and 3456×2234, two release takes of the packed crowd view at each of 2,000, 5,000 and 10,000 bodies report tick, extraction, ordering, upload bytes, sprite-pass GPU time, whole-frame time and shaded pixels over screen pixels, with backing extent, build and load. The check requires the Crowd trace's retained digests at ticks 120 and 240 in each take, and ties measurements in that interval to the rendered submissions and tick publications of the same replay. Timings flag the design's tripwires for investigation. Record: crowd replay cost under load.
items.ask: Do the cost takes draw the retained Crowd trace through the crowd view at its normal packing and sprite size? Can the check reject V1 field samples and samples from a run other than the measured replay, even when the row counts and timing fields match? Is the pass based on workload identity and record completeness, with reported times used as tripwires?

items.statement: In Chrome, two release takes of the packed crowd view at each of 2,000, 5,000 and 10,000 bodies report tick, extraction, ordering, upload bytes, sprite-pass GPU time, whole-frame time and shaded pixels over screen pixels, with backing extent, build and load. The check requires the Crowd trace's retained digests at ticks 120 and 240 in each take, and ties measurements in that interval to the rendered submissions and tick publications of the same replay. Timings flag the design's tripwires for investigation. Record: crowd replay cost under load.

In real time on the Mac the crowd of 10,000 reads clearly: players, enemies and projectiles can be told apart at a glance, the horde moves as one smooth mass, nothing flickers where bodies overlap, a body clearly lower on the screen is in front of the one it overlaps, a spawn and a death are clean, and a hit flash and a projectile's glow show in the thick of it.
items.inspect: Capture the crowd view at 10,000 with T2 engine capture: in `realtime` mode at 1920×1080, at least twenty seconds from a view of the whole crowd and twenty from a view close on one player, and `fixed` stills of both views at 3456×2234. Judge consecutive frames at 1x and the stills, whole and in native-size crops of the densest overlap, a player, and a projectile hit.

items.statement: In real time in Chrome the crowd of 10,000 reads clearly, moves smoothly and does not flicker where bodies overlap.
items.inspect: Capture the crowd view at 10,000 in Chrome with T2 engine capture in `realtime` mode: at least twenty seconds from a view of the whole crowd and twenty from a view close on one player. Judge consecutive frames at 1x, whole and in native-size crops of the densest overlap and a player.

items.statement: On the iPhone simulator the sprite scene runs through the iOS shell: the test card's aligned region is exact against the CPU reference, the game's entities are drawn as world rows, the compiled passes hold nothing 3D, and the scene keeps drawing after a rotation and after going to the background and back. Function only: no speed is claimed.
On the simulator's screen the sprite scene is upright in both orientations and inside the screen's bounds, with the card's texels square.
items.inspect: Take `simctl` screenshots in portrait and in landscape, beside the engine's capture of the same held frames. Judge each whole and in native-size crops of the card. Function only.

items.statement: The engine crates name no game's type, both proof scenes draw through the public sprite interface alone, and the sprite pass can run a second time in a frame with another target, view and row list.
items.ask: Does `thrum-render`, `thrum-asset`, `thrum-asset-gpu` or `thrum-cook` name a type, constant or sheet of the V1 game, the crowd or SWARM? Do the sprite scene and the crowd view reach the pass only through the interfaces the design lists? Does the pass take its target, view and rows as inputs, with no state that assumes one instance a frame?

items.statement: A guide linked from the creator guide shows how to declare a 2D scene, provide sheets, map components to world rows, supply a view and frame rows, choose layers and a band, and pick a scale for a window. It explains linear-light blending and the eight-sheet limit. The guide and public row documentation give the zero-band tie rule, frame-row placement in a banded inversion and higher-layer placement for marks that must cover a body.
items.ask: Do the guide's commands and code run at the claimed commit? Do the guide and public row documentation give the same frame-row placement as mechanism 4 for both zero band and its A, B, F example?

items.statement: The maturity ledger says what this module proved and what it did not.
items.ask: Do the ledger's rows for 2D keep implementation, correctness, visuals and device results apart? Do they name as not run: motion measured on the built-in panel itself, how values above white look on an EDR display, a physical iPhone, a Mac window on a display of density 1, Android, and any browser other than Chrome?

items.statement: The drawn overlap follows mechanism 4 for world rows A and B and two frame rows F and G whose layer and value match B. With band 1 and the retained A, B inversion at values 0.75 and 0.25, the same-layer order is F, G, A, B. At zero band it is B, F, G, A. Moving F and G to a higher layer puts both in front of the retained world order. The small Metal witness reads the submitted overlap pixels to distinguish these orders. Guard: mixed sprite-row ordering.

work_packages.quality_bar: Crowd legibility as in Vampire Survivors and Halls of Torment: with thousands on screen every enemy, projectile and player stays readable, the horde moves as one smooth mass at the display's refresh, and nothing flickers where bodies overlap. Pixel stability as in Celeste. A guide a game maker can follow without reading engine source, as Bevy's 2D examples are.
